title: Dedications
paragraphs: To my grandchildren, Alice and Ezra, who have learned to love walking in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī.
To my husband and best friend, Howard Z. Streicher, who brought me to this magical place in 1974 and loves all things Hawaiian.
This book is dedicated, especially, to the Hawaiians and early Polynesians who had the foresight to settle on this magnificent ‘āina. Mahalo piha.
In memory of my mother, Alice Acson, who loved walking in Waikīkī.

title: Foreword
paragraphs: Waikīkī and Neighborhoods: An Urban Walking Guide into History
Respecting the Wahi Pana Walk Waikīkī for your Health!
The history of Hawai‘i is opened up to you, as the life of Hawai‘i is revealed to you through these walks.
Venture into the wild side of the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī and its history: urban walks with good, sensible shoes!

It is suggested that you take these walks in cool weather, which means early mornings or late afternoons. Also, try to walk in the shade, which, generally, means makai-Diamond Head side in the mornings and mauka-‘Ewa side in the afternoons.

The first book about historic walks in Waikīkī appeared in 1983. I am proud to say that it was among the first books to describe the real Waikīkī, not just the glittery hotels and restaurants. Even historian and revered Hawaiian scholar, George S. Kanahele, the author of the definitive book on Waikīkī, Waikīkī, stated: “We should acknowledge Veneeta Acson’s book[] Waikīkī: Nine Walks Through Time, Island Heritage, 1983, certainly the precursor of the Historical Trail idea.”

The second book, which came out 20 years later, saw some changes including the disappearance of some old, charming buildings and structures, such as the original Halekūlani Hotel and Buckminster Fuller’s Geodesic Dome, which was replaced by the Kālia Tower of the Hilton Hawaiian Village.

Since then, several other books about Waikīkī especially some beautiful “coffee table” books, have been published. Much has happened in those intervening years, not only in Waikīkī, but also in the United States and our world.
Other sites are still standing, but much improved and better integrated into Hawaiian life: the Kāhuna Stones; ‘Āinahau Park/Princes Ka‘iulani Park; and Kūka‘ō‘ō Heiau.

This book, the third book about historic walks, 20 years later, is expanded to include the neighborhoods mauka of the beach area of Waikīkī, all within the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī. The neighborhoods of Mō‘ili‘ili, Kaimukī, and Mānoa Valley offer a rich panoply of early Hawaiian life as well as bustling life today: Mō‘ili‘ili with its underground caverns and lizard mo‘olelo (legends); Kaimukī and its Pu‘u o Kaimukī,

the high point (literally and figuratively) of the walk where you can see not only the Wai‘anae mountain in the west, but also the islands of Lāna’i and Moloka‘i in the east; and Mānoa Valley, which proudly presents the only restored intact heiau in Waikīkī at the Mānoa Heritage Center, along with marvelous Mānoa Falls, Lyon Arboretum, Mānoa Chinese Cemetery, and the fabulous University of Hawai‘i.
The walks to Mānoa Valley and to the main campus of the University of Hawai‘i follow McCully Street.
The walks to Kaimukī, Mō‘ili‘ili, and the lower UH campus walks proceed along Kapahulu Avenue.

For Waikīkī residents and visitors, the walks into the ahupua‘a begin or go along Kapahulu Avenue (on the Diamond Head side) or McCully Street (on the ‘Ewa side). However, for residents who live mauka of the canal, the walks can begin further inland. Just be sure to read the introductions to each walk before you proceed.
